extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy and ethics (Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative distinctions about friendship (its kinds, causes, permanence, and social/political analogues) as found in a didactic classical treatise chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as virtue / necessary / honourable
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is either itself a virtue or connected with virtue; it is most necessary for life and is honourable (we praise those fond of friends; having numerous friends is creditable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that no one would choose to live without friends even if they had all other goods; rich or powerful people particularly need friends (to do and receive kindnesses, to keep prosperity). Some even treat 'good man' and 'friend' as synonymous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship's practical benefits across life stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship helps the young to keep from error, helps the old with attention and action-deficiencies, and aids those in their prime in devising and executing plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship functions as moral and practical support appropriate to different ages: corrective for youth, compensatory for old age, enabling collaboration in adulthood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship implanted by nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship appears natural: parent-offspring, kin, members of the same tribe or nation show natural friendly dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations of animals and human travel (man is friendly to man) support that friendly affections are a natural impulse, not purely artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as bond of social communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is the bond of social communities; legislators seek to secure it, sometimes even more than Justice because unanimity resembles friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political stability and the suppression of faction depend on fostering friendship/unanimity among citizens; friendship underpins larger social unities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between Friendship and Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where people are in Friendship, Justice is not required; yet just persons still need Friendship as an additional principle; the truest justice partakes of the nature of Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship and Justice overlap in object‑matter and the persons they bind; friendship makes certain juridical interventions unnecessary, and stronger friendship can intensify obligations beyond impersonal justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual goodwill and mutual knowledge requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For true Friendship it is requisite that parties have kindly feelings, wish one another good (for one of the accepted motives), and that these kindly feelings be mutually known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being kindly-disposed towards someone without mutual recognition does not complete Friendship; mutual knowledge of reciprocal goodwill is part of the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objects/motives of Friendship: good, pleasure, useful
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects (causes) of Friendship are threefold: what is good, what is pleasurable, and what is useful — yielding three corresponding species of Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy grounds later evaluative claims: each motive produces different qualities, permanence, and social forms of Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship of utility is result-oriented and unstable
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships motivated by utility love one another only insofar as some good/advantage accrues; they are friendships of result and liable to dissolve when advantage ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common among the old or those pursuing profit; intimacy is limited or absent; hospitality is often classed here; such friendships last only so long as the useful circumstance continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship of pleasure is impulsive and changeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships motivated by pleasure love for what is enjoyable to themselves; common among the young, they form and dissolve quickly as pleasures change, and often involve desire for close companionship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because youthful passions and momentary pleasures shift rapidly, these friendships are less permanent though they seek intimate intercourse; love (eros) is often an extreme form of this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect Friendship (based on virtue) is stable and altruistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Friendship subsists between good people who wish one another's good for the other's sake; it is permanent because goodness has a principle of permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect friends are good both abstractly and relatively to one another, are mutually pleasurable and useful in the right way, and wish good to their friends disinterestedly. Such friendships are rare and require time and intimacy to develop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutuality of benefit from same source increases permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships are most permanent when the same result accrues to both parties from the same source (e.g., two men of like pleasantry), rather than asymmetric relations like lover/beloved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reciprocal and symmetric sources of pleasure or advantage strengthen the tie; asymmetric dependencies (one who loves and one who merely receives) are more fragile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad men cannot be truly disinterested friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad men may form friendships by pleasure or profit, but they lack the stability and self-regard that grounds disinterested Friendship; only the good can be friends for the other's sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad men have no settled principle of stability and often seek advantage or delight in wickedness; their 'friendships' are contingent and less trustworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and intimacy required for genuine Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Desire for Friendship may arise quickly, but genuine Friendship requires proof, time and intimate acquaintance (proverbially 'eating the requisite quantity of salt together').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid interchange of friendly acts may indicate a wish to be friends but not real Friendship; testing by time and shared experience is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living together and shared pleasures characterize companionship-Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Living with one another, taking pleasure in each other's company and sharing objects of pleasure are characteristic of the Friendship of companionship; absence impedes acting out Friendship and prolonged separation can destroy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friends must be mutually pleasurable companions; morose or elderly persons who provide little pleasure are less apt to engender such Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect friendship cannot be widespread; number limited
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a perfect friend to many is not possible; perfect Friendship is an excessive state naturally limited to one primary object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like love, deep virtuous Friendship tends to focus on a single or very few persons due to requirements of closeness, time, and intimate knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendships between superior and inferior differ and must be proportional
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships where one party is superior to the other (father/son, ruler/ruled, husband/wife) are of distinct kinds; the feeling of Friendship should be proportionate to the parties' relative merits or usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The better or more beneficial person may be the object of stronger feeling; equality in Friendship is a proportional equality rather than strict numeric parity (contrast with Justice). Proper reciprocal duties make such friendships equitable and stable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality and similarity (especially of goodness) bind friends
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity and a due proportion of equality — especially similarity in goodness — are ties of Friendship; good men, being stable, are stable friends and avoid wronging one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarity in virtue produces mutual pleasure, usefulness, and permanence; dissimilar extremes in goodness or prosperity may break the sense of entitlement to be friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is coextensive with communion / social association
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship corresponds to the extent of social Communion: friends in each communal relation (brothers, comrades, fellow-citizens) differ in degree, and 'the goods of friends are common' because Friendship rests upon Communion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different communal aims (voyage crew, war comrades, religious clubs) produce different friendships and corresponding principles of Justice and mutual obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogies between political constitutions and types of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Political constitutions (Kingship, Aristocracy, Timocracy) and their corruptions have likenesses in domestic/familial relations: e.g., father/sons as Kingship, Persian paternal despotism as Despotism, husband/wife like Aristocracy or Oligarchy when misordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle maps constitutional forms to household relations to show how rule, distribution of goods, and relative equality shape the character of friendships and obligations within those relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendships of result are named by resemblance but lack full friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships based on pleasure or profit are called friends by resemblance to perfect friendship but are 'friends as a matter of result' rather than truly for the other's sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such secondary friendships may be socially called 'friends' (e.g., political alliances), but they lack the permanence, mutual altruism, and moral state characteristic of true virtuous Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship dissolves when its motivating cause vanishes
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships founded on pleasure or profit commonly part when the pleasure or advantage ceases, because their existence was relative to changing circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially true for utility-based friendships (shopkeepers, alliances) and pleasure-based friendships when tastes/pleasures change with age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire to be object of Friendship functions as honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people desire to be the objects of others' Friendship as a form of honour (they prefer being honoured/fêted), and thus may seek flatterers rather than genuine reciprocal Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pursuit of honour is often instrumental (to secure future benefit) rather than for its own sake; genuine friends entertain the sentiment more than merely being its object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship is a moral state, not merely a feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertaining friendly sentiment is like a feeling, but Friendship itself is a state involving moral choice: friends wish good to their friends for their sakes, not merely as a sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mothers who delight in the feeling of friendship toward adopted children even without reciprocation; moral disposition (state) distinguishes true Friendship from mere kindly feeling.
